case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of the mother's parental rights, holding the petitioner proved by clear and convincing evidence that the children were deprived, that the causes of deprivation were likely to continue, and that the children would probably suffer serious harm.
key_cases.relevance: Confirms that the deprivation adjudication is the gateway decision on which later petitions depend.
key_cases.quote: To terminate a parent's rights, the children must first be deprived.

key_cases.holding: The court reversed a default termination of parental rights and remanded, holding a parent who had responded to the petition could not have her rights terminated without evidence, and that the court could not rely on prior-proceeding records without satisfying the requirements for judicial notice and affording an opportunity to be heard.
key_cases.relevance: Filing a petition does not relieve the agency of proving its allegations with evidence at hearing.
key_cases.quote: In parental termination proceedings, due process requires clear and convincing evidence before parental rights may be terminated.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding the juvenile court correctly applied the law and that clear and convincing evidence supported findings of deprivation, likely continuation of the causes of deprivation, resulting harm, and reasonable reunification efforts.
key_cases.relevance: Defines the proof the agency must marshal when it petitions to move from temporary custody to termination.
key_cases.quote: These elements must be established by clear and convincing evidence.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding the findings that the child was deprived, that the causes and conditions of deprivation were likely to continue, and that continued deprivation would probably cause serious harm were each supported by clear and convincing evidence and were not clearly erroneous.
key_cases.relevance: Defines what the agency must ultimately be able to prove when it files a petition seeking termination rather than temporary custody.
key_cases.quote: termination of parental rights requires satisfaction of a three-pronged test which the party petitioning for termination must prove by clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed an adjudication that a ten-year-old was deprived by reason of parental alienation and psychological maltreatment, holding the finding of deprivation by clear and convincing evidence was not clearly erroneous and that the juvenile court had not improperly merged the divorce-related custody dispute with the deprivation proceeding.
key_cases.relevance: The clean citation for the burden the agency carries when it files a deprivation petition, decided the same day as T.J.L. and applied without the distortion the brief flagged elsewhere.
key_cases.quote: A juvenile court's finding of deprivation must be supported by clear and convincing evidence.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that an unwed father was entitled as a matter of due process to a hearing on his fitness before his children could be taken from him, and that Illinois's presumption of unfitness for unwed fathers, while affording a hearing to every other parent, denied him equal protection.
key_cases.relevance: Establishes that the State's petition must lead to an adjudication of the particular parent's fitness, which is the constitutional root of North Dakota's requirement that a deprivation or need-for-protection petition be proven at a hearing.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that, as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him

key_cases.holding: The court retained jurisdiction and remanded with instructions to issue a new order based only on the trial evidence, holding that even when the statutory elements of N.D.C.C. § 27-20.3-20(1)(c) are established the juvenile court retains discretion whether to terminate, and that it abused that discretion by relying on evidence outside the record and on a clearly erroneous count of the child's nights in foster care.
key_cases.relevance: Confirms that the agency's petition must be decided on the evidentiary record made at the hearing, and that a court may not fill gaps by taking judicial notice of material outside that record.
key_cases.quote: Therefore, when the statutory elements to terminate parental rights are met, the court has discretion, but is not required, to terminate parental rights.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of a father's parental rights under the current juvenile chapter, holding that N.D.C.C. § 27-20.3-20(1)(c)(2) requires only that the child have been in foster care at least 450 nights and does not require that 660 nights have elapsed since the child entered care.
key_cases.relevance: Shows the sequence under ch. 27-20.3 from placement to a child-in-need-of-protection adjudication to a permanency hearing to the termination petition, and what the agency must prove at each step.
key_cases.quote: The plain language of the statute requires the child be in care for at least 450 nights.
